meta.blurb: For her big school project, seventeen-year-old Zee Rahman chooses an old question: did a caretaker really steal a charity's Fun Run money? With her friend Callum, she follows the evidence to a surprising and powerful person.
meta.bible: Zainab Rahman: called Zee, seventeen, in her last year at Hallam Grove Sixth Form; careful and brave; her project asks whether Jim Kettle really stole the money. Callum Brandt: her friend, good with computers and records; keeps three backups. Aisha Rahman: Zee's mother. Ms Okoye: the teacher in charge of the project; teaches that a good question is one that evidence can answer. Mrs Dunne: the retired school secretary of thirty-one years; kept the alarm slips. Ron Heath: a retired police constable. Jim Kettle: the school caretaker in 2015, sacked and never charged; now lives in Kinloch in Scotland. Pam: Jim's sister in Millbridge, who kept his bus ticket. Alan Fenwick: treasurer of the Fun Run in 2015, now chair of governors, a councillor, owner of Fenwick Gardens and a candidate for mayor; the villain. Mr Gale: the former headmaster; his wife was ill; saw Fenwick's green car at the school gate on Sunday morning. Sam Greaves: the young Detective Constable at Ashby police station. Mr Singh: a records manager at Beacon Alarms. Ashby: the town. Hallam Grove: the school and sixth form. Millbridge: the town where Jim's sister lives. Ashby Gazette: the local newspaper. Companies House: the public record of companies. Facts: the Ashby Fun Run was on Saturday 10 October 2015 and raised thirty-one thousand pounds in cash for a children's hospice; the safe had two keys, held by Jim and by Fenwick; Jim locked the safe at half past one and set the alarm (user one) at ten to two, then caught the twenty-past-two bus to Millbridge; Fenwick (user seven) switched the alarm off at ten past seven on Sunday and on again at eight; Fenwick told the police the alarm was off all weekend; Fenwick Gardens received a director's loan of thirty thousand pounds on 9 November 2015. Voice and tone: a clear, fair-play teen detective story; no violence; honest and hopeful.

B1B2: Zainab Rahman, who everyone called Zee, was seventeen and in her last year at Hallam Grove Sixth Form. She had to choose one big question for her project, and she had no idea yet what it would be.
Their teacher, Ms Okoye, told the class that a good question was one that evidence could answer. She said that guesses and gossip were no use, and that proof was the only thing that counted.
At the town library, Zee turned the pages of an old local newspaper from eleven years before. One headline stopped her at once: Fun Run Money Vanishes From School.
The Fun Run had raised thirty-one thousand pounds in cash for a children's hospice. The money had been locked in the safe at Hallam Grove, but on Monday morning the safe was empty.

The paper said that the school caretaker, Jim Kettle, had a key to the safe and had been sacked. He was never charged with anything, but he left Ashby soon afterwards and nobody had heard of him since.
Zee asked her friend Callum Brandt to help, because he was brilliant with computers and records. They set up a case board in his garage with string, photographs and an old whiteboard.
Before they began, Zee and Callum wrote some rules on the whiteboard. They would ask permission, tell people why they were asking, keep every recording, and check every fact twice.
At supper Zee told her mother, Aisha, about the project. Aisha said that old stories can hurt real people, and that Zee must be kind as well as clever.
Mrs Dunne, the old school secretary, poured tea for Zee and Callum in her living room. She said that Jim Kettle was the most honest man she had ever known, and that she had told the police so.
Mrs Dunne explained that the school alarm had given every person with a code a number. The alarm printed a little paper slip every time someone switched it on or off.
Mrs Dunne said that Alan Fenwick, the Fun Run's treasurer, had told the police the alarm was off all weekend for repairs. She had never believed this, but nobody had asked her.

Zee wrote two lines on her notepad and thought hard about what Mrs Dunne had said. If the alarm had really been on, there must be a record of who switched it off, and that would contradict Mr Fenwick.

Ron Heath, a retired police officer, told them that the safe had been opened with a key and that nothing had been broken. He said the case was closed, unsolved, because there was nothing to prove who had done it.
Heath said that only two keys had opened the safe, and that Jim Kettle had held one of them. Jim also had money problems at the time, which was why the police had looked at him first.
That evening Zee and Callum looked up Alan Fenwick on the internet. He was now the chair of governors at Hallam Grove, a town councillor, the owner of Fenwick Gardens, and a candidate for mayor.

Zee suspected the old headmaster, Mr Gale, because he had retired so suddenly, but he showed them a letter about his wife's illness. Then he said that he had seen Fenwick's green car at the gate on Sunday morning.
Callum searched the public company records on the internet. They showed that Fenwick Gardens had received a director's loan of thirty thousand pounds on 9 November 2015, four weeks after the theft.
Alan Fenwick agreed to meet them in his office, and he was friendly and charming. He said that it was old, sad news and that poor Jim Kettle had obviously taken the money.
As they walked out to the car park, Callum said something strange. In forty minutes Mr Fenwick had not asked them a single question about what they had found.

The next day Ms Okoye took Zee aside and said that Mr Fenwick had phoned the headteacher. Zee was being told to change her topic, but Ms Okoye also said, very quietly, that she should carry on carefully.
On Thursday Zee logged on to the school computer and found that her project folder was empty. Every file and photograph had disappeared, and nobody could explain how.
Callum only smiled when he heard about the missing files. He had saved every note, scan and recording in three different places, and he gave Zee a spare drive to hide at home.
A few days later, someone let down both tyres on Zee's bicycle outside the school. Her mother grew worried, but Zee told her that this proved they were asking the right questions.
Callum worked out that Jim Kettle now lived in a small village in Scotland called Kinloch. Zee wrote him a careful letter that explained who she was and why she was asking.
Jim Kettle's reply came within a week, and it was only three lines long. It said that the Fun Run money had broken his life and that he begged her to leave it alone.
Zee called the number on the letter, and Jim finally agreed to a video call. He said that he had locked up on Saturday afternoon and then caught a bus to visit his sister Pam.
Jim told Zee that he had put the money in the safe at half past one on Saturday. He had set the alarm at ten to two and then he had left for the bus.
Jim's sister Pam, it turned out, had kept the bus ticket from that Saturday in a drawer. She sent Zee a photograph of it, and it showed the time, twenty past two, and the date.
Mrs Dunne spent two days searching the boxes in her garage. At last she found a dusty folder with the old alarm slips inside, because she had always kept copies of everything.
The slips showed that user one had set the alarm at ten to two on Saturday. On Sunday morning user seven had switched it off at ten past seven and back on at eight.
Zee and Callum laid the slips beside the old police notes. The alarm had not been off all weekend, which meant that Mr Fenwick had told the police something untrue.

Callum emailed Beacon Alarms, the company that had fitted the system, and a manager named Mr Singh replied. He said the events for user seven were still on file, but only the police could ask for them.
With Ms Okoye beside her, Zee took her evidence to Detective Constable Sam Greaves at Ashby police station. He was cautious, but he copied everything and promised to look into it.
One evening Alan Fenwick appeared at Zee's front door with a bunch of flowers for her mother. Smiling, he said that he would hate to see a talented girl ruin her future with an ugly accusation.
After Mr Fenwick had gone, Aisha put the flowers in the bin and held her daughter's hands. She said that Zee must do it properly, and that she would stand beside her all the way.
Zee, Callum and Ms Okoye planned to present the project at the school's end-of-year showcase. They invited Mrs Dunne, Mr Gale, Jim by video and Detective Constable Greaves.
On the night of the showcase, the school hall was full. Alan Fenwick, as chair of governors, sat in the front row in his best suit, ready to give out the prizes.
Zee stepped up to the podium and read out her question in a steady voice. Then she showed a timeline of the Fun Run weekend on the screen behind her.
Zee showed the bus ticket on the screen and then Jim Kettle appeared by video. He said clearly that he had been on a bus to Millbridge when the money was taken.
Zee then showed the alarm slips on the screen, with the times and the numbers. In the front row Alan Fenwick stopped smiling, and he sat very still.
Alan Fenwick jumped to his feet and shouted that it was slander, and that the slips were forged. The hall gasped, and the head teacher looked from one of them to the other in alarm.
Mrs Dunne rose from her seat and said that she had kept those slips in her own folder for eleven years. She had dated each one herself, and she was prepared to swear to it in any court.

Mr Gale stood up and said that he had seen Mr Fenwick's green car at the school gate that Sunday morning. Then Callum put up the company records, showing a thirty-thousand-pound loan four weeks later.
Alan Fenwick looked around the silent hall and then, for the first time, he lost control. “I was going to put it back,” he said in a shaking voice, and then he realised what he had said.
Detective Constable Greaves walked quietly down the aisle from the back of the hall. He spoke a few low words to Alan Fenwick, who rose and went with him without another sound.
On the screen Jim Kettle was wiping his eyes with the back of his hand. Zee told him that she was sorry that it had taken so long, and that she was glad that he had trusted her.

Some weeks later, the police charged Alan Fenwick with theft, and his garden centre was sold to repay the money. The hospice received its thirty-one thousand pounds at last, and Jim Kettle came back to Ashby to visit.
Ms Okoye gave Zee the highest grade for her project. She said that the best part of it was not the ending, but the care with which Zee had gathered every piece of evidence.
Zee and Callum sat in the garage one last time and looked at the old whiteboard. They agreed that feelings had started the question, but only evidence had answered it.
Zee picked up the marker and wiped the board clean. Then she wrote a new question in her neatest handwriting, and Callum, smiling, reached for his laptop.
C1C2: Zainab Rahman, whom everybody called Zee, sat in the sixth-form library with an empty page and a deadline that was creeping closer by the day. Her teacher had asked every student to choose one large question and spend a year answering it with proper evidence, and Zee wanted hers to matter. She had no idea yet that the question was already waiting for her in an old newspaper.

Ms Okoye, the teacher in charge of the project, walked slowly between the desks and told the class that a good question is one that evidence can answer. Guesses and gossip, she said, were worth nothing, and a student who could not show where a fact came from had no right to repeat it. Zee wrote the sentence in her notebook, underlined it twice, and never forgot it.

At the town library on Saturday, Zee spooled through eleven years of the Ashby Gazette, hoping for a topic and expecting only flower shows and council meetings. Halfway through the autumn of 2015 a headline made her stop and read it again, because it said that the money from the town's charity Fun Run had vanished from a school safe. The school involved, to her astonishment, was her own, the very one where she now studied and sat her lessons.

The article explained that the Ashby Fun Run of 2015 had raised thirty-one thousand pounds in cash for a children's hospice, and that the money had been locked in the safe in the school office for the weekend. When the staff arrived on Monday morning, the safe was open and empty, with no broken lock and no broken window. The whole town, said the newspaper, was in shock, and the hospice had already begun to wonder how it would pay for its summer programme.

The caretaker, a man called Jim Kettle, had held one of the two keys to the safe, and within a week the school had dismissed him and the whole town had decided that he was guilty. He was never charged, because the police had found no proof, yet he left Ashby soon afterwards under a cloud, and nobody had heard of him since. Zee closed her notebook, looked at the clock above the shelves, and knew exactly what her question for the year would be.

Zee told her friend Callum Brandt about her question, and he agreed to help before she had even finished the sentence, since nothing delighted him more than a mountain of records. Within an evening they had turned his garage into an incident room, with a whiteboard, a ball of red string and a cork board covered in photocopied articles. Callum, who rarely spoke more than he needed to, wrote the title in capital letters: DID JIM KETTLE REALLY DO IT?

Before they began, Zee insisted that they write a few rules on the whiteboard, because Ms Okoye had taught her that evidence gathered carelessly is worse than none at all. They would ask permission before they interviewed anyone, say plainly what the project was about, keep every recording safe, and check each claim in two separate places. Callum added a fifth rule in smaller letters, which said that if they found out Jim Kettle was guilty, they would say so.

At supper that evening Zee told her mother, Aisha, about the Fun Run and the missing money, and Aisha listened with the thoughtful frown she wore when she was weighing something carefully. She warned her daughter that old stories are not museum pieces, that they still hurt real people who are living with them, and that Zee must be kind as well as clever. Zee promised that she would be careful with people's feelings, and she meant every word, although she did not yet know how hard it would be.

Mrs Dunne, who had been the school secretary for thirty-one years, poured tea for Zee and Callum in her cluttered living room and said that she had been waiting a long time for someone to ask. Jim Kettle, she declared, was the most honest man she had ever worked with, and she had told the police exactly that, although nobody had seemed interested. She spoke with the stubborn loyalty of someone who had been proved right and never thanked.

Mrs Dunne explained that the school's alarm system had assigned each authorised person a user number. Every time it was switched on or off, a small printer in the office had spat out a slip of paper recording the number and the time. She had a list of the numbers in her old diary, she said, and Callum, who had gone very still, asked whether anyone had ever looked at the slips.

Mrs Dunne's face hardened as she said that Alan Fenwick, the treasurer of the Fun Run, had told the police that the alarm had been switched off all weekend for repairs. She had never believed this for a moment, because the engineer had not come until the following week, but nobody had thought to ask the school secretary. In the whole affair, she said bitterly, the people who knew the facts were the ones who were never consulted.

Zee wrote two short lines on her notepad, pressed the pen hard against the paper, and underlined the second one twice. If the alarm had in fact been switched on that weekend, then somewhere there was a record of who had switched it off, and that record would contradict the account the treasurer had given. She did not say it aloud, because Ms Okoye had also taught her that a theory is only a theory until something supports it.

Ron Heath, a retired police constable with a weathered face and a patient way of speaking, told them over his garden gate that the safe had been opened with a key and that nothing had been forced. The alarm, he recalled, had been switched off according to Mr Fenwick, which meant that no record existed, and so the case had faded away unsolved. He seemed relieved that somebody still cared about the case after so many years, and he offered them tea and all the time they needed.

Heath explained that two keys had fitted the safe, one held by the caretaker Jim Kettle and the other by the Fun Run's treasurer, who was Alan Fenwick, a respected local businessman beyond suspicion. Jim, he admitted, had been struggling with debts at the time, and in a small town that had been enough to point every finger at him. He added, thoughtfully, that he had always felt uneasy about how quickly the matter was closed.

That evening Zee and Callum looked up Alan Fenwick and discovered that he had prospered remarkably since 2015. He was now the chair of the governors at Hallam Grove, a councillor who smiled from every second noticeboard, the owner of a large garden centre called Fenwick Gardens, and a candidate in the coming election for mayor. It was impressive, and it was also, as Callum observed, quite a lot of luck for one man.

Zee had begun to suspect the former headmaster, Mr Gale, because he had retired in a hurry only weeks after the theft, and she and Callum visited him with a certain nervousness. He showed them, with great dignity, the letters about his wife's illness that had forced him to leave. Then, almost as an afterthought, he mentioned that he had driven past the school at half past seven on the Sunday morning, and that Alan Fenwick's green car had been parked at the gate.

Callum, who could navigate public records like a sailor reading the stars, found the filings for Fenwick Gardens on the Companies House website, which anyone may read for free. They showed that on 9 November 2015, four weeks after the Fun Run, the firm had received a director's loan of thirty thousand pounds, a sum that the director could not easily have found by ordinary means. Zee stared at the screen and said that it proved nothing yet, but that it made her heart beat faster.

Alan Fenwick agreed to meet them in his office at the garden centre, and he welcomed them with the warm, practised smile of a man accustomed to votes. It was old and sad news, he said with a sigh, and poor Jim Kettle had so obviously taken the money that the police had hardly needed to investigate. He offered them a plate of biscuits and a donation to any other project they cared to choose.

As they crossed the car park, Callum said quietly that the most remarkable thing about the meeting had been the thing that had not occurred. In forty minutes of conversation Alan Fenwick had not asked them a single question about what they had discovered, or whom they had spoken to, which struck Callum as the behaviour of a man who already knew. Zee glanced back and saw the councillor standing at his window, watching them leave.

The next morning Ms Okoye took Zee aside in an empty classroom and said, in a lowered voice, that the chair of governors had telephoned the headteacher to complain about a student who was raking up the past. Officially, Zee was being told to change her topic, but Ms Okoye added that she personally believed that a question asked honestly should be answered honestly. Zee thanked her warmly and resolved to be more careful than ever, though she did not yet know how closely she was being watched.

On Thursday Zee logged on to the school network and discovered that her project folder, which had held weeks of notes, scans and interview recordings, was completely empty. The technician could find no explanation, and no one at the school office could say who had touched it, but a cold suspicion lodged in her mind like a splinter. She walked to Callum's garage that afternoon with her jaw set and her fists clenched, determined that nobody would erase the truth so easily.

Callum merely smiled when he heard the news, because he had copied every note, scan and recording into three separate places on the very first night. He handed Zee a small spare drive to keep hidden in her bedroom, and he explained, with the dry humour that few people ever saw, that a good detective is a pessimist who also owns a backup. It was the first time all week that she had laughed, and the sound of it echoed pleasantly off the walls of the garage.

A few days afterward, Zee found both tyres on her bicycle slashed flat outside the school gates, in broad daylight, with no one willing to admit that they had seen a thing. Her mother, who collected her from school in the car that afternoon, was visibly frightened, but Zee insisted calmly that when people begin to interfere with a question, it generally means the question is a good one. Aisha did not argue with her daughter in the car, but she did not smile either, and her hands were tight on the wheel all the way home.

After a week of patient searching, Callum worked out that Jim Kettle now lived in a tiny village called Kinloch, on the far side of Scotland, where he worked quietly as a handyman. Zee wrote him a careful, honest letter, explaining who she was, what her project was about, and that she was prepared to listen to whatever he wished to say, however painful. She posted it on Friday morning, walked back to school through the drizzle, and tried very hard not to hope too much.

Jim Kettle's reply arrived within the week, and it was only three lines long, written in a hand that shook slightly on the page. The affair, it said, had broken his life, his name and his marriage, and he begged her not to open the wound again for the sake of a school project. Zee read it three times and felt sick, but she did not feel that she should stop.

Zee telephoned the number at the bottom of the letter, and after a long, difficult conversation Jim Kettle agreed to talk to her on a video call that Sunday. On the screen he looked older than his years, a tired man with large, careful hands, and he told her that he had locked the safe and set the alarm on Saturday afternoon. Then he had caught the bus to his sister Pam in Millbridge, and he had not returned to Ashby until late on Sunday night, knowing nothing at all.

Jim remembered every detail of that Saturday with painful clarity, from the cash bags piled on the office desk to the click of the safe door closing at half past one. He had set the alarm at ten to two, walked out of the school gates, and caught the twenty-past-two bus to Millbridge, and he had not seen the building again until the Monday morning when the police had been waiting. He told it all in a flat, tired voice, as if he had said it a thousand times to an empty room.

Jim's sister Pam, who was one of those people who keep everything, found the faded bus ticket from that Saturday in a biscuit tin and sent Zee a photograph of it that same evening. It showed the date, the route from Ashby to Millbridge and the departure time of twenty past two, which meant that Jim had been miles away from the school at the time the safe was supposedly emptied. It did not prove who had taken the money, but it proved where Jim had not been.

Mrs Dunne, who had never thrown away a piece of paper in her life, spent two entire days searching the boxes in her garage, muttering under her breath. At last she found a dusty folder labelled in her own neat hand, and inside it lay the little printed slips from the school alarm, which she had kept because she did not trust computers. The dates of that October weekend were among them, and her hands trembled as she carried the folder into the kitchen.

The slips told a story that nobody had read in eleven years: user one had set the alarm at ten to two on the Saturday afternoon. User seven had switched it off at ten past seven on the Sunday morning and on again at eight, and it had stayed on until Jim Kettle cancelled it on the Monday. Mrs Dunne turned to her old diary, ran her finger down the list of numbers, and read aloud the name beside seven, which was Alan Fenwick.

In the garage, Zee and Callum laid the slips beside the notes from Ron Heath and the details from Mr Gale, and for a long time neither of them spoke. The alarm had not been off for the weekend, as Alan Fenwick had insisted to the police, and the very man who had said so had been the one to switch it off at ten past seven on Sunday morning. Callum picked up a marker and wrote it on the whiteboard in letters a foot high, and for once his hand was not quite steady.

Callum emailed Beacon Alarms, the company that had installed the school's system, and within a day a records manager named Mr Singh answered with the careful politeness of a man who is not allowed to say too much. The old events were still held in an archive, he confirmed, including entries for user seven on that weekend, but they could be released only to the police or to the school's own governors. Since the chair of governors was the man in question, Zee thought that left only one choice.

With Ms Okoye sitting protectively beside her, Zee took the folder to Detective Constable Sam Greaves at Ashby police station and laid out the evidence page by page, as steadily as she could. He was a young, thoughtful officer who warned her that a case eleven years cold would take time, but he copied every document, asked a dozen sharp questions and promised that he would look. It was the first time in the whole project that Zee felt the weight lift a little.

One evening Alan Fenwick appeared at the Rahmans' front door with a large bunch of flowers, a gentle smile and an air of fatherly concern. He told Aisha that he hated to see a talented young woman throw away her future by spreading ugly accusations, and that a charge of slander could follow a girl to every university and every job. Zee, standing quietly in the hallway, had already pressed the record button on her phone.

When Alan Fenwick had gone, Aisha took the flowers outside and put them in the bin, and then she came back and took her daughter's hands in both of her own. If Zee was going to do this, she said, her voice thick with feeling, she must do it properly and in the open, and her mother would be standing beside her in the front row. Zee, who had braced herself for another warning, found that she could not speak, and she simply put her arms around her mother.

Together Zee, Callum and Ms Okoye planned to present the project at the school's end-of-year showcase, an evening when every student displayed a year's work before the governors, the staff and the parents. They invited Mrs Dunne and Mr Gale to attend in person, arranged for Jim Kettle to join on a screen from Scotland, and quietly asked Detective Constable Greaves to sit at the back. It was a gamble, Zee admitted to Callum, but it was a gamble made in the open, in front of everyone, and that made all the difference.

On the evening of the showcase the school hall was packed to the doors, with parents holding programmes and students pacing nervously beside their displays. Alan Fenwick, in the front row in a crisp suit, shook hands with the head, laughed at a joke and prepared to present the prizes, apparently unaware of what was about to happen. Zee, standing in the wings with her notes shaking, found her mother's eyes in the audience and breathed out.

Zee walked to the podium, laid her notes down, and read out her question in a clear, steady voice: did Jim Kettle really steal the Fun Run money? Behind her, the screen displayed a timeline of the weekend of the tenth of October, with the key hours marked in blue, and the audience, who had been whispering, fell silent. She explained her rules, her sources and her promise to follow the evidence wherever it led.

Zee displayed the photograph of the faded bus ticket, with its date and its departure time of twenty past two, and then she introduced a guest who joined them from Scotland. Jim Kettle appeared on the great screen above the stage, thinner and greyer than anyone remembered, and said in a firm voice that on that Saturday afternoon he had been on a bus to Millbridge, far from the school. There was a murmur of surprise in the hall, and several people turned to look at the front row, where Alan Fenwick sat very still.

Next Zee displayed the old alarm slips on the screen, enlarged so that every number and time could be read from the back of the hall. She explained, step by step, that user one had set the alarm on Saturday and that user seven had switched it off on Sunday morning at ten past seven. In the front row the smile faded slowly from Alan Fenwick's face, and his hands closed on the programme in his lap.

Alan Fenwick sprang to his feet and shouted, in a voice that had lost all its warmth, that this was slander and that the slips were obviously forged by a silly girl with an overactive imagination. The hall gasped, the head teacher half rose from her seat, and a hundred heads turned between the stage and the front row. Zee gripped the edge of the podium and found, to her surprise, that she was not afraid.

Mrs Dunne rose from the middle of the hall, small and straight in her best coat, and said in the voice of a woman who had addressed children for thirty-one years that the slips were real. She had kept them in her own folder for eleven years and written the date on each one herself, she declared, and she was perfectly prepared to swear to it in any court. For once, nobody in the hall was brave enough to interrupt Mrs Dunne, and even the head teacher sat back down in silence.

Mr Gale rose beside Mrs Dunne and said, with the gravity of a man who has waited too long, that he had seen Alan Fenwick's green car at the school gate that Sunday morning. Then Callum, on cue, projected the company filings, which showed a director's loan of thirty thousand pounds paid into Fenwick Gardens on the ninth of November. The silence in the hall was now so complete that one could hear the clock ticking above the stage.

Alan Fenwick looked around at the silent faces, at Mrs Dunne's folder, at the bus ticket on the screen and at the girl on the stage, and something finally gave way inside him. “I was going to put it back,” he said in a hoarse voice, and in the next heartbeat he understood what he had confessed. For a long moment there was no sound in the hall at all, not even the rustle of a programme or the scrape of a chair.

Detective Constable Greaves rose from his seat at the back of the hall and walked quietly down the long aisle, with the whole audience following him with their eyes. He spoke a few low words to Alan Fenwick, who got slowly to his feet like an old man, and the two of them left through the double doors without another sound. It was over, though nobody in the hall quite knew how to begin breathing again.

On the great screen Jim Kettle covered his face with his large hands, and when he looked up again his eyes were bright with tears and astonishment. Zee, speaking to him across the whole hall, said that she was sorry it had taken eleven years, and that she would always be grateful that he had trusted a stranger with his story. The whole audience rose to its feet as one, and the clapping began, slowly at first and then like a great wave breaking.

A few weeks later the police charged Alan Fenwick, and the garden centre was sold to repay what had been taken, together with a great deal of interest. The children's hospice received its thirty-one thousand pounds at last, and the council issued a public apology to Jim Kettle. Jim himself came back to Ashby for a single afternoon, where Mrs Dunne met him at the station with a flask of tea and a large slice of cake.

Ms Okoye awarded Zee the highest grade that the project could earn, and in her comments she wrote that the finest thing about it was the care with which every piece of evidence had been gathered. She said that Zee had proved that a question asked patiently could outweigh a powerful man's smile. Zee kept that page folded carefully in her wallet for years afterwards, and she took it out whenever she doubted herself.

Zee and Callum sat in the garage one last evening, looking at the whiteboard that was now covered with ticks, and Callum said, in his dry way, that he had expected a lot of luck and had found mostly paperwork. Zee laughed and agreed that instinct might begin a question but only evidence could close one, and that the paper slips in Mrs Dunne's folder had said more than any accusation. They shook hands solemnly, like two old colleagues at the end of a long career, and then they switched off the garage light.

Zee picked up the marker, wiped the whiteboard clean, and stood for a moment looking at the white space where the old question had been. Then she began to write a new one in her neatest hand, a question about a lost painting that her grandmother had mentioned only that morning, and Callum, smiling, reached for his laptop. Somewhere in a town full of old stories, another small piece of the truth was waiting to be found.
